title: EAP: Encrypted IMSI Memory Bug
description:
Added complete CertificateSerialNumber string match
logic to prevent malformed strings.  Replaced strlen()
call with mbstowcs() to account for wide characters to
prevent incorrect character counts.  Added 3GPP realm
string matching logic to optional Realm token in Encr.
IMSI identities.
Closes #18129.

notes.body:
added 1 commit
  • ea747a09 - EAP: Encrypted IMSI Memory Bug
[Compare with previous version](/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/7141/diffs?diff_id=414418062&start_sha=2f33674020a51d82803a0c67cb63683aaa5392a4)

1. The reason why there are extra characters is specifically because `tvb_get_string_enc(pinfo->pool, tvb, offset, size, ENC_ASCII);` always generates good UTF-8 (which we use internally when possible) but with the 'ENC_ASCII' parameters replaces all the non ASCII characters with the UTF-8 REPLACEMENT CHARACTER, U+FFFD, which is three bytes (0xEF 0xBF 0xBD) in UTF-8. This is probably what you want as you expect it to use ASCII characters, correct?

However, `mbstowcs` is not the best solution:

1. `mbstoswcs` behavior is locale-dependent. If the locale is not UTF-8 based (which can happen on some systems) then this doesn't work.
2. You may need to add `#include <stdlib.h>` to get `mbstowcs` on all possible platforms and compilers.
2. C11 does not guarantee that `mbstoswcs` has the behavior where one is allowed to pass in NULL for the destination to get the number of characters. (This is possibly an oversight, as `mbstowcs_s` and `mbsrtowcs` do both specify this. Still, cf. 7.22.8.1 to 7.29.6.4.1 and K.3.6.5.1, even in C17/C18.) POSIX and Microsoft do both work this way.

I suggest using [g_utf8_strlen](https://developer-old.gnome.org/glib/unstable/glib-Unicode-Manipulation.html#g-utf8-strlen), since we require glib, the string is guaranteed to be a valid null-terminated UTF-8 string, and that function is not locale-dependent.

added 116 commits
  • ea747a09...7c96053f - 115 commits from branch wireshark:master
  • f5decdcd - EAP: Encrypted IMSI Memory Bug
[Compare with previous version](/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/7141/diffs?diff_id=425851459&start_sha=ea747a0997f53fc1cfb97fadd0effa79b12bc7b0)

To quote #18129:

> `strlen()` mishandles wide character values that can show up in these identity strings

If there are "wide character values" in these identity strings, then "wide character values" presumably means "non-ASCII character values encoded using some multi-byte encoding, such as UTF-8 or an MBCS".

If so, then the strings should be fetched using the encoding in question, e.g. 

```
    identity = tvb_get_string_enc(pinfo->pool, tvb, offset + 1, size - 1, ENC_UTF_8);
```

What's going on here is that the values are expected to be ASCII, so it's being fetched as ENC_ASCII. However, the fuzzed version has non ASCII characters, which  `tvb_get_string_enc` replaces with the UTF-8 REPLACEMENT CHARACTER, which is is three bytes (0xEF 0xBF 0xBD).

So the fetched string is longer in bytes than the original data, the fetched data is split into tokens, and there are a few places where the dissector wants to get the byte offset of the original data.

There *should* never be wide characters actually in the protocol; this is all to avoid crashing on fuzzed or other erroneous data.

> There *should* never be wide characters actually in the protocol

So you're saying that 1) the strings are always ASCII and thus 2) @msweant is mistaken in his analysis?

Yes, as transmitted the Encrypted IMSI is BASE64:

From [ETSI TS 133 402 V17.0.0 14.1](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/133400_133499/133402/17.00.00_60/ts_133402v170000p.pdf):
>The last step in the generation of the temporary identities consists on converting the concatenation above to a printable string using the BASE64 method described in section 4.3.2.4 of RFC 1421 [41]

And the other parts are ASCII as well.

I.e., there are two reasons why a string of 8-bit octets containing one-octet ASCII characters might also contain octets with the 8th bit set:

1. Those octets are either "extended ASCII" characters (e.g., ISO 8859/1) or parts of "extended ASCII" characters (e.g., UTF-8, or some MBCS).
2. Those characters are garbage either accidentally or deliberately inserted.

Thus, they aren't necessarily indications of the presence of "wide characters".

In these cases, they're indications of deliberate insertion of garbage, that being what "fuzzing" is.

Perhaps we should have `tvb_get_string_enc()` should be passed a pointer to a boolean, and set that to TRUE if the string is valid in the specified encoding and FALSE if it's not valid in that encoding, so that code knows not to try to parse the string if it's not valid.

For the particular case, using `tvb_ascii_isprint()` beforehand could work, but passing in an optional boolean pointer like that makes sense, since determining if the encoding is valid generally means doing almost all of the work of converting it.

Another option is a parameter (or different function) that causes it to return early indicating that the string is not valid instead of proceeding on (and putting in REPLACEMENT CHARACTERS), for an optimization in cases with unexpected characters.

@johnthacker identified a clear path where we check for a valid ASCII string before pulling the string into its own buffer and begin tokenization and dissection.  Should the identity string prove non-compliant with ASCII, then we will throw a warning, post the entire string to eap.identity, and stop further dissection.  This will flag non-ASCII identities but still allow the user to analyze the identity string without the benefit of reading the tokenized portions (specifically referring to encrypted IMSI identities).
